entries.author: James Smith, Developed Markets Economist
points: OBR sees the deficit falling to 3.4% of GDP in 2027 from 4.2%, almost entirely through fiscal drag from frozen thresholds.
Net loosening is small (about 0.2% of GDP this year), mostly temporary energy support; the £312bn gross financing requirement was below most expectations.
Departmental budgets and defence are pushed to the Spending Review; the implied 2.6% a year real cuts for unprotected departments look unlikely to happen.
entries.quote: doesn't do anything that could make life harder for the Bank of England
entries.title: UK Chancellor sticks to script but leaves more questions than answers

entries.author: Helen Miller, Director
points: Broadly the Budget many expected: the Chancellor accepted higher borrowing over five years in the face of bad economic news.
Welcomed the commitment to consolidation, but very tight public service spending plans are its weak point.
Higher borrowing leaves less scope to absorb future bad news; little in the Budget to move the dial on growth.
entries.quote: has an Achilles' heel in the form of very tight plans for public service spending
entries.title: Initial response to the Autumn Budget (via House of Commons Library)

points: Mild fiscal loosening, mainly through energy bills and council tax, gave households some breathing space.
The buffer against the fiscal rules fell from £23.6bn in March to £14.5bn.
No attempt to bring debt-to-GDP down in the medium term, so the public finances depend on good fortune.
entries.quote: leaves the UK government more exposed to renewed market scrutiny
entries.title: Budget response (via House of Commons Library)

points: Cost of living support was poorly targeted and spread thinly across the income distribution.
Little was done to repair the damage to the public finances from higher debt interest costs.
The Chancellor has left himself little room to absorb further negative news.
entries.quote: remarkable for its lack of action, rather than its radicalism
entries.title: Spread Thin: response to the Autumn Budget (via House of Commons Library)

entries.author: Thomas Pugh and Jack Wellard
points: A rise to 4% was almost certain; expect at least one more hike in 2027 and no cuts until 2028.
The Budget did little to bring gilt yields down, and headroom shrank from about £24bn to £15bn, leaving the Chancellor exposed to further rises in rates or inflation.
Growth slows over the winter; GDP growth of 1.5% in 2026 and real household disposable income up only about 0.3% in 2027.
entries.quote: inflation above 4% is simply too high for the Bank to sit back and ignore
entries.title: The Week Ahead: UK interest rates going higher, the only question is how high

entries.author: Michiel Tukker, Senior UK & Eurozone Rates Strategist
points: After repeated losses on dovish positions, the front end carries a risk premium beyond the fundamentals; markets price more hikes than ING expects.
Two-year rates should ease in the first half of 2027 as energy prices fall, with a bigger dovish shift in the second half.
Persistent deficits and heavy gilt supply keep upward pressure on long yields and steepen the curve; recent QT changes mainly help 30-year gilts.
entries.quote: we therefore see rates lower across the curve, but only once inflation risks settle
entries.title: A delayed landing for GBP rates

entries.author: James Smith, Developed Markets Economist
points: Bank Rate up from 3.75% to 4%; the Bank sees inflation peaking at 4.9%, mostly energy, and wants more data on second-round effects.
ING expects one more hike by February (December if energy re-spikes), then cuts from late 2027 or early 2028 towards 3.25%.
Markets price about a 50:50 chance of a December hike, about four hikes over the next year and no cuts after that, which ING thinks is too hawkish.
entries.quote: this is a hike solely about the risks
entries.title: Hawkish Bank of England hikes rates, and there's more to come

entries.author: Sanjay Raja, Chief UK Economist (via MoneyWeek)
points: The hike adds restriction to a stance that was already restrictive; Governor Bailey also played down a long sequence of rises.
Financial conditions have tightened since March, so the case to go much further is weaker than in 2022.
Expects one more rise to 4.25%, in December or February.
entries.quote: we don't think this is the start of a long hiking cycle
entries.title: Today's hike is not the start of a long hiking cycle

entries.author: Suren Thiru, Chief Economist (via MoneyWeek)
points: Strong backing for the hike and the tone of the minutes suggest further increases are probable.
US-Iran hostilities hold the key: unless energy prices retreat, more hikes move from a risk to a real prospect.
With the Bank forecasting inflation to keep rising, a February hike looks increasingly likely.
entries.quote: the path for interest rates is hanging in the balance
entries.title: November hike signals a sizeable shift in direction

entries.author: James Smith, Developed Markets Economist
points: Base case: a February hike, then a cut before end-2027 as weak wage growth lets the Bank look through inflation of about 4.5% in early 2027.
Risky call: Prime Minister Burnham calls a snap election; markets would likely dislike it because it exposes questions about long-term borrowing.
Bold call (not the base case): the UK agrees an EU customs union, which ING thinks would strengthen sterling.
entries.quote: Brexit is unpopular, but rejoining the EU still looks remote
entries.title: Brexit, elections and rate hikes: 3 calls for the UK

themes.text: Commentators called the 28 October Budget cautious and largely as expected. ING noted gilt financing came in below expectations, but headroom against the fiscal rules fell to roughly £15bn, leaving less room to absorb bad news.
themes.title: Budget passed without a gilt scare

themes.text: The Bank raised Bank Rate to 4% on 5 November, driven by energy prices, with inflation projected to peak near 5% in 2027. Most see one more hike by February; markets price more than economists expect.
themes.title: First Bank Rate rise since 2023

themes.text: Nearly every note ties the rate outlook to oil and gas prices. If energy eases, ING and Deutsche Bank expect a short cycle with cuts from late 2027; if not, the ICAEW sees further hikes becoming a real prospect.
themes.title: Energy and the Middle East set the path

themes.text: ING flags a possible snap election under Prime Minister Burnham as its 'risky call' for 2027, which it thinks markets would dislike because it reopens questions about long-term borrowing.
themes.title: Political risk is back in view
